title: Your work files are encrypted and there is a ransom note
lede: Files will not open. Names have changed to something unfamiliar. There is a text file or a full-screen message with a countdown and a payment address, and the same thing is starting to happen on the shared drive.

blocks.text: Files will not open. Names have changed to something unfamiliar. There is a text file or a full-screen message with a countdown and a payment address, and the same thing is starting to happen on the shared drive.

items: Every minute the machine stays connected, more shared and backup data is encrypted. Disconnection is the highest-value action available and it is available immediately.
This is almost always an organisational incident, not a personal embarrassment. Concealing it for an hour is the most expensive thing an individual can do here.
Modern ransomware usually copies data out before encrypting it, so this is a data breach as well as an outage — which has legal reporting duties in many jurisdictions.
Paying is a decision for the organisation with legal advice, and often does not restore data. It is never a decision for the person at the keyboard.

items.detail: Pull the cable, turn off wi-fi. Do this before anything else, including finishing this list.

items.move: Do not shut down or restart
items.detail: Memory can hold keys and forensic evidence. Disconnect, leave it powered, and report.

items.move: Tell IT or security right now
items.detail: By phone, not email. Say the word ransomware. Speed of reporting is the main variable you control.

items.move: Disconnect external drives and unmount cloud sync
items.detail: USB drives and synced folders are prime targets and often the only surviving copy.

items.move: Warn colleagues on the same share verbally
items.detail: Get people off the affected drive before it spreads further through open sessions.

items.move: Photograph the ransom note with your phone
items.detail: The strain identification matters for recovery, and you may not be able to reach the screen later.

items.say: "I have a ransomware infection on my machine. I have disconnected it from the network and left it powered on. Files on the P drive are also affected."
"Get off the shared drive now — there is an active encryption incident. IT knows."
Say plainly what you did — the attachment, the link, the file. Blame is far less costly to you than a delayed timeline.
"That is a decision for legal and the board, and law enforcement should be consulted first."

items: Trying to clean it yourself with a downloaded tool.
Restoring from backup onto a machine that is still infected — that destroys the backup too.
Waiting to see if it stops. It does not.
Hiding it because you clicked the link. That single hour of silence is what turns an incident into a catastrophe.
Expect password resets across the organisation, and treat any credential stored on that machine as compromised.
Personally: check whether personal accounts were logged in on that device, and change those passwords from a clean device.
Verify that backups are actually restorable and genuinely offline. Most failed recoveries are failed backups.
Expect breach-notification obligations if personal data was on the machine. That is legal territory, not IT territory.
